doc.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024

title: Jazz as revolutionary truth-telling; Cornel West
summary: Jazz embodies multiplicity; his heroes include Carla Bley, Chico O'Farrill and Mingus; he recounts the Four Questions recording with Cornel West.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: what it means to be American, which means to embrace multiplicity. The real definition of America is a nation borne out of many, many, many people. The nation was not founded by white Europeans, it was already here with indigenous beings and the indigenous people are the Americans who were already here. So the United States, the history of many people coming together to form this union. And that’s to me is what jazz is. Jazz at its best represents the multiplicity of cultures, the trans-culturation of humanity. We are Irish, we are German, we are Cuban, we are Mexican, we are Scandinavian, we are Puerto Rican, we are all those things and the best part of the United States is when we don’t try to isolate the internationalism. The best part of the United States is not when you’re American but when you embrace all of what America is. And I feel that same way about jazz. Global Jazz Studies is just the way to understand that Mother Africa filtered the sources. Some of the sources were Middle Eastern, some of them were South Asian, some of them were European. Some of them all got together, all of these ingredients came together in Mother Africa where they cooked and basted and were spiced and you stirred the pot, and also all these influences became a uniquely African event that was then brought to the indigenous world by the horrific cataclysm called the slave trade. And so I think that Global Jazz Studies is very important because if we think of jazz as invented on August 3 in New Orleans in 1923 then we’ve really, really actually done a tremendous disservice to the real revolutionary and transformative power of this music, which is that it is the music that demands equal voice for all human beings. Jazz is the most revolutionary music that I can think of. And when I think of my heroes, in addition to Carla Bley and Chico O’Farrill, I think of Charles Mingus. I think of people who demanded that the truth tellers, that the truth be told, that Governor Faubus be called out. I think that, when I think of my heroes they are the people that insist that jazz — it’s funny, I did a recording with Cornel West that won a Grammy called “Four Questions.” And I wrote a concerto basically for Cornel West’s oratory. And we were backstage at The Apollo at the premier and we were talking about jazz and we were talking about how some people insist that jazz is this, born here, and this is what it is. And we were laughing because it’s so different. Jazz is the ultimate revolutionary power of truth telling, bold, unashamed, unembarrassed. Truth demands a telling of the truth. And we looked at each other and all of a sudden we both — it don’t mean a thing if it ain’t got that sting. We just started laughing.
